events.excerpt: Description A few small nit cleanups on the synchronizer component in consensus. Behavior change: fetch_blocks_from_peers now returns as soon as no request is in flight, instead of idling until the 4s FETCH_FROM_PEERS_TIMEOUT. This affects two cases: no request was sent because every selected block was already locked, or the last outstanding request failed with no peer left to retry on. In both cases no further network request is sent, and a failed request still waits the full 2s request timeout, so periodic runs cannot repeat faster than every ~2s on failures. The only new cost is local: while all selected blocks are locked, the scheduler polls get_missing_blocks at its default 200ms cadence instead of every 4s, which is the same cadence it already uses during fast successful sync. Added a test covering both cases. Test plan CI/PT Release notes Check each box that your changes affect. If none of the boxes relate to your changes, release notes aren't required. For each box you select, include information after the relevant heading that describes the impact of your changes that a user might notice and any actions they must take to implement updates. Protocol: Nodes (Validators and Full nodes): gRPC: JSON-RPC: GraphQL: CLI: Rust SDK: Indexing Framework: Co-authored-by: Claude Fable

After the update, those invisible objects can apparently make the printed document disappear too. Microsoft said: "The issue was observed when printing Microsoft Word documents using the Windows Graphics Device Interface (GDI), but printing from other applications might also be affected." events.excerpt: A Democratic takeover of Congress may look like bad news for the industry, but Bitwise Chief Investment Officer Matt Hougan believes the bigger picture tells a different story. While the election could bring short-term market volatility, Hougan said that the changing demographics of Congress matter more to crypto’s long-term prospects than which party holds power. Importance of Demographics The latest election put Democrats in control of both houses of Congress, with Elizabeth Warren likely to become chair of the Senate Banking Committee. Given her history of opposing crypto, the development has raised concerns about what could come next for the industry. Hougan, however, does not see the election as a major setback. According to the lobbying group Stand With Crypto, the incoming Senate has 51 pro-crypto members, compared with 52 in the outgoing Congress. In the House, at least 241 members have received an A or B rating on crypto policy, which gives them a solid majority in the 425-member caucus. The more interesting change is the age of the lawmakers entering Congress, according to Hougan. Incoming senators are, on average, 14 years younger than those leaving. events.excerpt: This release contains bugfixes and improvements to the stacks-node and stacks-signer binaries, ensuring more consistent block production. This release is compatible with chainstate directories from 4.0.x. This release is recommended for all Stacks node and signer operators. This release includes the following changes: https://github.com/stacks-network/stacks-core/blob/4.0.6/CHANGELOG.md ⚠️ Breaking Changes Unused speculative tries from mining and block-proposal validation are no longer persisted. MARF databases automatically migrate to schema 4 on writable open, removing the legacy mined_blocks table and its stored tries. Older binaries cannot open upgraded databases, including in read-only mode; upgrade chainstate inspection and snapshot tooling alongside the node. Signers in this release rely on the node's new GET /v3/blocks/:block_id/view endpoint and the canonical field on /v3/sortitions to release a signed block that a Bitcoin fork has orphaned. Against an older node a signer stays safe but never releases such a block, which can stall a tenure after a reorg. Upgrade the stacks-node before, or together with, its signer. Removed the stackslib::chainstate::stacks::index module; the MARF now lives in the stacks-marf crate. Downstream library consumers should import from stacks_m

events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. Because leanVM has no authority, a leanVM bug can’t break Ethereum’s security or halt the chain. At the same time, leanVM runs on mainnet under real load, so
events.headline: EIP Draft: Run leanVM aggregation in shadow mode alongside BLS until PQ/AI day

events.excerpt: United Airlines has become the latest company to slap restrictions on unauthorized third-party AI agents, warning that the bots could make unintended purchases, expose customer data, or bypass checks requiring human acknowledgment. The airline announced restrictions covering both its own digital platforms and indirect access through travel agencies and aggregators, with changes to its booking, ticketing, and distribution policies. United says automated actions could violate aviation regulations, citing the requirement for a human acknowledgment during check-in that bags contain no banned substances. A bot cheerfully ticking the box isn't quite the passenger confirmation it has in mind. And then there is the worry that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles." United would also rather customers use its own app than turn third-party assistants loose on its systems. events.excerpt: by Fei Wu. This work was partially conducted during my internship at the EF. I thank my mentor @misilva73 for helpful discussions and comments. Overview Previously, we have presented our analyses of the equilibrium and dynamic simulation of EIP-7999’s multidimensional fee market, comparison with the post-Glamsterdam one-dimensional fee market . We combine and extend these analyses into a paper: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum . In the previous post , we studied three one-dimensional benchmarks: the baseline (64-gas-per-byte floor and CPSB = 1530 ), floor-adjusted + EIP-8368 , and floor-adjusted + EIP-8372 . The strongest is floor-adjusted + EIP-8372 given the current resource demand , which we call the normalized benchmark in the paper: the transaction floor price is adjusted to each propagation allocation, and EIP-8372 scales CPSB and the state gas limit by a common factor, so that regular gas and state gas reach their targets at the same base fee in equilibrium. It keeps the EIP-1559 target-to-limit ratio of 1/2 and the EIP-1559 update rule. Under block-level demand variation, it delivers 151.9M–177.9M execution gas per block, but regular gas and normalized state gas both stay below their targets on average, giving 86.0–88.1 GiB
events.headline: More Meters or More Prices? One- vs. Multi-dimensional Fee Mechanisms on Ethereum

events.excerpt: Video game controllers have come a long way from the days when a vibration motor was enough to make the action in the game feel real. Modern controllers can simulate everything from the recoil of a gun to the resistance of pulling a bowstring — but there's still something missing. They can't reproduce the finer details of touching and handling objects in a virtual world. Researchers from Hunan University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences are looking to change that with ElectroPad , a modified PlayStation 5 controller that makes virtual objects feel more realistic. ElectroPad uses a technique called electrotactile stimulation. By sending carefully controlled electrical pulses through electrodes in contact with the skin, it can create localized sensations that mimic textures, edges, and shapes. The idea is to let players feel the surface of a virtual object as their character interacts with it, rather than simply experiencing a generic vibration. To make this possible, the researchers developed a pair of custom covers that fit over the handles of Sony's DualSense controller. Each cover is just 2 millimeters thick but contains 190 individually addressable electrodes, giving the complete controller an impressive 380 stimulation points. events.headline: ElectroPad Makes Virtual Worlds Feel More Real
